title: Opioid Use Disorder: Agonist Treatment Is First-Line Care
bottomLine: Opioid use disorder is a treatable chronic condition. Current Canadian guidance considers buprenorphine and methadone standard first-line opioid agonist treatments; withdrawal management alone is not adequate treatment because relapse and overdose risk remain high.
recognize: Loss of control, craving, continued use despite harm, hazardous use and physiologic dependence can occur, but prescribed physical dependence alone is not OUD.
differentiate: Tolerance and withdrawal can occur during appropriate opioid therapy without compulsive use or functional harm.
assessment: Assess opioid type and route, fentanyl exposure, overdose history, withdrawal, pregnancy, other sedatives, pain, mental health, housing, treatment goals and naloxone access.
workup: Use urine drug testing selectively to inform care, not punish; assess pregnancy, infection and organ function when clinically relevant.
management: Offer buprenorphine or methadone as first-line OAT and slow-release oral morphine as a second-line option when appropriate; integrate harm reduction, psychosocial support and treatment of coexisting pain/mental illness.
medicationSafety: Buprenorphine initiation strategy must account for recent opioid exposure and precipitated-withdrawal risk; methadone has accumulation, QT and interaction risks requiring careful titration.
counselling: Use person-first language, offer take-home naloxone and discuss safer-use strategies even when abstinence is not the patient's goal.
followUp: Continue OAT as long as benefit persists; if discontinuation is desired after sustained stability, use a slow individualized taper.
examTrap: Detoxifying a patient from opioids and discharging without offering ongoing opioid agonist treatment.
oneLinePearl: Withdrawal management treats withdrawal; OAT treats opioid use disorder.
sourceBasis: CRISM National Opioid Use Disorder Guideline 2024 update

title: Opioid Overdose: Ventilate, Naloxone, Observe the Recurrence Risk
bottomLine: Opioid overdose is respiratory failure. Support ventilation immediately, give naloxone and reassess repeatedly because potent or long-acting opioids can outlast naloxone.
recognize: Reduced consciousness, slow or absent respirations and miosis are typical, but pupils may vary with mixed overdoses.
differentiate: Hypoglycemia, stroke, sedative overdose and head injury can mimic altered consciousness; naloxone response supports opioid contribution but does not exclude co-ingestion.
assessment: Assess airway and breathing first, glucose, trauma, co-ingestants, opioid type/timing and intention of overdose.
workup: Use ECG, acetaminophen level and other toxicology tests when the exposure is uncertain or mixed; routine broad drug screens rarely change emergency management.
management: Provide bag-mask ventilation or advanced airway support as needed and titrate naloxone to restore adequate ventilation, not necessarily full wakefulness; observe for recurrent toxicity.
medicationSafety: Large naloxone doses in opioid-dependent patients can precipitate severe withdrawal, but this is preferable to untreated respiratory arrest; titration is appropriate when ventilation can be supported.
counselling: Offer naloxone, OAT and harm-reduction linkage after overdose.
followUp: A nonfatal overdose is a high-risk transition point and should trigger rapid addiction follow-up.
examTrap: Waiting for naloxone to work before providing ventilation to an apneic patient.
oneLinePearl: In opioid overdose, oxygenation and ventilation come before toxicology certainty.

title: Alcohol Use Disorder: Screen, Diagnose, Treat—Do Not Just Advise Less
bottomLine: High-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder deserve active treatment. Use validated screening, assess withdrawal risk and offer evidence-based medications and psychosocial treatment rather than relying on advice alone.
recognize: Loss of control, craving, role impairment, hazardous use and continued drinking despite harm support AUD.
differentiate: High-risk drinking does not automatically equal AUD, but both can cause health harm.
assessment: Quantify standard drinks and pattern, prior withdrawal/seizure, liver disease, pregnancy, medications, mental health, other substances and treatment goals.
workup: Use liver tests, CBC, electrolytes and other testing when clinically indicated; biomarkers do not replace history.
management: Use brief intervention for lower-severity unhealthy use and evidence-based AUD pharmacotherapy such as naltrexone or acamprosate when appropriate, plus psychosocial support; manage withdrawal safely.
medicationSafety: Naltrexone is inappropriate with current opioid use and needs hepatic context; acamprosate requires renal dosing.
counselling: Use Canada's current alcohol-and-health guidance: less alcohol means lower health risk, without implying that any threshold makes drinking risk-free.
followUp: Track drinking goals, cravings, function and medication response.
examTrap: Telling a patient with severe AUD to stop drinking abruptly at home despite a history of withdrawal seizures.
oneLinePearl: Before recommending abstinence today, ask whether stopping today could trigger dangerous withdrawal.
sourceBasis: Canadian guideline for high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder 2023
Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health

title: Alcohol Withdrawal: Seizure and Delirium Risk Are Time-Critical
bottomLine: Alcohol withdrawal can progress from tremor and autonomic hyperactivity to seizures and delirium. Risk-stratify using history and clinical state, give thiamine and appropriate benzodiazepine-based treatment, and use monitored care for high-risk withdrawal.
recognize: Symptoms begin after reduction or cessation and include tremor, anxiety, sweating, tachycardia, nausea and insomnia.
differentiate: Withdrawal delirium must be distinguished from sepsis, head injury, hepatic encephalopathy and other delirium causes.
assessment: Ask daily intake, last drink, prior severe withdrawal, seizures/DTs, comorbidity, pregnancy, other sedatives and social supports.
workup: Check glucose, electrolytes including magnesium, liver function and other tests based on comorbidity; use symptom scales only in patients who can participate reliably.
management: Use benzodiazepines according to a validated withdrawal pathway, thiamine before or with carbohydrate when deficiency risk exists, fluids/electrolytes and monitored admission for high-risk cases.
medicationSafety: Antipsychotics do not treat the underlying GABA-withdrawal physiology and should never replace adequate benzodiazepine therapy in severe withdrawal.
counselling: After stabilization, connect withdrawal care directly to AUD treatment to reduce repeated detox cycles.
examTrap: Using CIWA scores mechanically in a delirious noncommunicative patient who cannot validly answer the scale.
oneLinePearl: Withdrawal scales support clinical care; they do not replace it.

title: Benzodiazepine Dependence: Taper, Do Not Abruptly Stop
bottomLine: Long-term benzodiazepine use can cause tolerance, dependence, falls and cognitive impairment. Abrupt discontinuation can cause seizures and severe withdrawal, so deprescribing requires an individualized gradual taper.
recognize: Withdrawal includes anxiety, insomnia, tremor, perceptual disturbance and seizures.
differentiate: Return of baseline anxiety and true physiologic withdrawal can overlap; timing relative to dose reduction helps.
assessment: Assess agent, dose, duration, co-prescribed opioids, alcohol, falls, cognition, sleep and reason for original prescribing.
workup: Routine drug levels are not useful; medical testing is guided by complications and co-ingestion.
management: Use shared decision-making, gradual dose reduction and non-drug treatment for insomnia/anxiety; high-dose or complicated dependence may need specialty care.
medicationSafety: Opioid and benzodiazepine co-use substantially increases respiratory-depression risk.
counselling: Explain that dependence is a pharmacologic adaptation, not a moral failure.
followUp: Pause or slow taper when clinically appropriate rather than forcing a rigid schedule.
examTrap: Abruptly stopping a long-term benzodiazepine in a frail older adult because it is on a potentially inappropriate medication list.
oneLinePearl: Deprescribing a benzodiazepine is a taper, not a switch-off.

title: Stimulant Use: Cardiac, Psychiatric, and Harm-Reduction Risks
bottomLine: Cocaine and methamphetamine can cause ACS, arrhythmia, aortic disease, hyperthermia, agitation and psychosis. Acute treatment is syndrome-based while longer-term care uses harm reduction and evidence-based psychosocial addiction treatment.
recognize: Tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, agitation, chest pain and paranoia are common acute features.
differentiate: Primary psychosis, serotonin toxicity, alcohol withdrawal and thyroid storm can overlap.
assessment: Assess chest pain, temperature, neurologic symptoms, hydration, psychosis/suicide risk, route of use, adulterants and polysubstance exposure.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, CK, electrolytes and imaging when acute complications are suspected.
management: Treat hyperthermia aggressively, use benzodiazepines for severe sympathomimetic agitation and manage cardiac/neurologic emergencies according to standard pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid relying on a positive urine screen to date intoxication or prove current impairment; results can outlast clinical effects.
counselling: Discuss contaminated supply, safer use and naloxone because illicit stimulants may contain opioids.
followUp: Offer addiction and mental-health follow-up rather than treating each intoxication as isolated.
examTrap: Diagnosing current stimulant intoxication from urine toxicology alone when the clinical syndrome does not fit.
oneLinePearl: Toxicology screens detect exposure; bedside physiology determines toxicity.
sourceBasis: Canadian stimulant-use and emergency toxicology practice resources

title: Tobacco and Nicotine Dependence: Offer Treatment Every Time
bottomLine: Tobacco dependence is a chronic relapsing condition. Brief advice plus pharmacotherapy and behavioural support substantially improves quit success; a relapse is a treatment signal, not a reason to stop offering help.
recognize: Time to first cigarette, daily quantity, cravings and past quit attempts help estimate dependence.
differentiate: Nicotine vaping may reduce exposure to combustion for some adults who smoke but is not harmless and creates distinct youth/pregnancy concerns.
assessment: Ask all nicotine products, readiness and goals, prior treatment response, pregnancy, cardiovascular and mental health history.
workup: No laboratory test is required for routine cessation treatment.
management: Offer combination nicotine replacement, varenicline or bupropion when appropriate plus counselling and follow-up; tailor to patient preference and contraindications.
medicationSafety: Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure and eating-disorder contexts; nicotine replacement is generally safer than continued smoking and pregnancy decisions should be individualized.
redFlags: Recent serious cardiovascular event requiring individualized plan
counselling: Use nonjudgmental language and identify specific triggers and coping plans.
followUp: Reassess within weeks of the quit attempt and after relapse.
examTrap: Waiting for the patient to ask for help before offering evidence-based cessation medication.
oneLinePearl: Every tobacco visit is a treatment opportunity, not a lecture opportunity.

title: Cannabis: Dose, Route, Impairment, and Vulnerability Matter
bottomLine: Cannabis effects depend on THC dose, route, frequency, age and psychiatric or cardiovascular vulnerability. Screen for cannabis use disorder, hyperemesis, psychosis risk, driving impairment and pregnancy rather than treating cannabis as uniformly benign or uniformly catastrophic.
recognize: Frequent high-THC use increases risk of dependence, cognitive impairment and psychotic outcomes in vulnerable people.
differentiate: Cannabinoid hyperemesis causes recurrent vomiting in chronic users and often improves only with cessation; cyclic vomiting has other causes.
assessment: Ask product THC/CBD, inhaled versus edible, frequency, driving, pregnancy, mental health, vomiting and treatment goals.
workup: No routine urine test is needed to diagnose cannabis use disorder; evaluate complications as clinically indicated.
management: Use motivational and behavioural treatments for cannabis use disorder; treat acute psychosis or hyperemesis supportively and recommend cessation when causally implicated.
medicationSafety: Cannabis plus sedatives or alcohol worsens impairment; edibles have delayed onset that increases unintentional overconsumption.
counselling: Use Canada's lower-risk cannabis principles and avoid moralizing.
examTrap: Using a positive urine cannabinoid result to prove that today's confusion is caused by acute cannabis intoxication.
oneLinePearl: THC can remain detectable long after the acute clinical effect is gone.

title: Harm Reduction: Keep People Alive While Treatment Goals Evolve
bottomLine: Harm reduction reduces death and infection without requiring abstinence first. Naloxone, sterile equipment, safer-use education, infection testing and low-barrier treatment are clinical interventions, not endorsements of drug use.
recognize: Overdose risk rises after periods of abstinence or reduced tolerance, with polysubstance use and with unpredictable illicit supply.
differentiate: Harm reduction and treatment are complementary rather than competing approaches.
assessment: Ask route, using alone, supply source, overdose history, injection sites, sharing equipment, pregnancy and treatment goals.
workup: Offer HIV, hepatitis and STI testing and vaccination based on exposure risk.
management: Provide naloxone and overdose response education, sterile equipment linkage, OAT when appropriate and wound/infection care without withholding services because use continues.
medicationSafety: Warn about combined opioid, alcohol and benzodiazepine respiratory-depression risk.
counselling: Encourage not using alone and test-dose strategies where locally supported, while explaining that no illicit supply is predictably safe.
followUp: Keep the door open after missed visits and re-offer treatment repeatedly.
examTrap: Refusing OAT or wound care until a patient proves abstinence.
oneLinePearl: Harm reduction is treatment that meets the patient before the ideal endpoint.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada harm-reduction resources

title: Substance Screening: Ask Everyone, Intervene to the Level of Risk
bottomLine: Routine nonjudgmental substance screening identifies unhealthy use before crisis. Brief intervention is appropriate for lower-risk unhealthy use, while a substance use disorder requires diagnosis and active treatment rather than repeated advice alone.
recognize: People may not disclose use when questions imply blame or legal consequence.
differentiate: Screening identifies risk; DSM-style clinical criteria diagnose a use disorder.
assessment: Use validated alcohol, drug and tobacco questions and assess function, safety, withdrawal, pregnancy and driving.
workup: Testing should answer a clinical question; routine toxicology screening without consent or purpose can undermine care.
management: Provide feedback and brief motivational intervention for risky use; offer medication and specialty/addiction care when a use disorder is present.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe sedating controlled drugs without understanding alcohol, opioid and benzodiazepine use.
counselling: Use autonomy-supportive language and ask what change the patient is willing to consider.
followUp: Re-screen and follow treatment goals longitudinally.
examTrap: Treating a positive screen as a diagnosis of addiction.
oneLinePearl: Screening finds risk; assessment defines the disorder.
sourceBasis: Canadian substance-use screening and brief-intervention resources
